Effective fire management systems are essential for early detection, rapid response, and mitigation of fire impacts. To address this challenge, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) integrated with advanced state-of-the- art deep learning techniques offer a transformative solution for real-time fire detection, monitoring, and response. This comprehensive survey critically examines recent advancements in vision-based fire management systems enabled by autonomous UAVs. It explores how baseline deep learning models, including convolutional neural networks, attention mechanisms, YOLO variants, generative adver- sarial networks and transformers, enhance UAV capabilities for fire-related tasks. Unlike previous reviews that focus on conventional machine learning and general AI approaches, this survey emphasizes the unique advantages and applications of deep learning-driven UAV platforms in fire scenarios. It provides detailed insights into various architectures, performance and applications used in UAV-based fire management. Additionally, the paper provides detailed insights into the available fire datasets along with their download links and outlines critical challenges, including data imbalance, privacy concerns, and real-time processing limitations. Finally, the survey identifies promising future directions, including multimodal sensor fusion, lightweight neural network architectures optimized for UAV deployment, and vision-language models. By synthesizing current research and identify- ing future directions, this survey aims to support the development of robust, intelligent UAV-based solutions for next-generation fire management. Disas- ters are broadly classified into natural and technological categories, with technological disas- ters including nuclear plant accidents, acts of terrorism, and hazardous material incidents, whereas natural disasters encompass floods, earthquakes, and fires. Fire is one of the most perilous disasters characterized by its rapid spread and destructive nature, making it chal- lenging to control within a short time frame. Fires are primarily caused by individual activi- ties, such as cooking in buildings, road construction, and smoking in forested areas, as well as natural factors like thunderstorms and global warming (Feng et al. 2019). Uncontrolled fires can have a profound impact on human life, businesses, ecology, and the environment at both global and local levels. In recent years, climate change has exacerbated the incidence of large-scale wildfires and hazardous fires across diverse landscapes, including forests, urban areas, and industrial sites (Dabous et al. 2024). This intensification is driven by rising global temperatures, prolonged heatwaves, earlier snowmelt, and altered precipitation pat- terns, all of which significantly increased the frequency, duration, and severity of wildfires across diverse ecosystems. Studies indicate that these factors have contributed to a marked increase in fire-prone days and an extension of fire seasons worldwide, particularly in Mediterranean and boreal regions (Farid et al. 2024; Bolan et al. 2025). The synergistic effects of these environmental stressors have resulted in more frequent mega fires, which are harder to control and more destructive to both ecological and human systems. Therefore, timely detection and effective fire intelligence systems are essential for successful firefight- ing and disaster response; however, these challenges continue to pose significant difficulties for society. Scalar sensor-based fire detection systems have several advantages, including cost-effectiveness, rapid fire detection, capabilities of early warning, ease in implementation and integration with other fire safety systems (Khan et al. 2022). Furthermore, sensor-based systems can provide nonstop environmental monitoring, minimizing the risk of undetected fires and allowing for early evacuation. However, sensor- based systems have certain limitations, such as generating false alarms due to smoking, steam, dust or cooking (Fonollosa et al. 2018). Sensors-based system response time to fire detection increases over time. Moreover, it is challenging to detect fires in the initial stages if the fire is far from the sensor-based system or growing slowly. Ensuring early fire detec- tion accurately and precisely is essential for fire management, and an alternative approach, such as a fire intelligence system, is required to overcome the limitations of sensor-based systems, such as false alarm rates. To tackle these challenges of a scalar sensor-based system, such as false alarms from steam, dust, or cooking emissions, an intelligence vision-based fire detection system was proposed, which provides wide coverage, requires no human intervention, offers a prompt response, and is ecologically robust. A vision-based fire detection system, such as closed- circuit television (CCTV) offers broad coverage and real-time fire detection using visual fire indicators, including flames and smoke (Ahn et al. 2023; Zhang and Geng 2024). This type of vision sensor verifies fire incidents and makes it easier to take action against fires (Li and Sun 2024). Nevertheless, it has also reduced the number of false alarms generated by scalar-based sensor systems (Li et al. 2024b). Despite this advantage, CCTV still has some limitations, the most important being limited area coverage and a fixed direction. To overcome this limitation, researchers are interested in finding the optimal solution for fire detection. Advancements in AI technology can assist in early fire detection and tackle the drawbacks of traditional vision-based methods. These advancements reduce the impact of fire on individual lives, financial losses, and ecosystem damage. UAVs have been proposed as optimal technology for vision-based fire management systems due to their enormous potential (Liz-López et al. 2024). UAVs integrated with advanced artificial intelligence tech- nologies are emerging as transformative tools in wildfire management. These AI-powered UAVs enable rapid, autonomous aerial surveillance, allowing early fire detection through real-time thermal imaging, smoke segmentation, and computer-vision techniques. Further- more, UAVs can fly to high-risk spots without the intervention of human beings and provide confirmation of fire with real-time updates for accurate planning and monitoring during firefighting, without threatening human lives (Afghah et al. 2019; Zhu et al. 2025b). For example, Pesonen et al. proposed a lightweight segmentation model trained using bound- ing box-guided supervision and foundation models, capable of detecting wildfire smoke at pixel-level accuracy and 25 frames per second using onboard UAV computing resources, which is ideal for remote areas lacking mobile connectivity (Pesonen et al. 2025). Beyond detection, predictive modeling has advanced significantly. The probability of fire (PoF) model, developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), integrates vegetation dryness, lightning activity, and human presence to forecast fire risk with greater spatial and temporal precision than traditional indices (Di Giuseppe et al. 2025; Centre 2025). These models, when deployed via UAVs, enhance situational awareness and support dynamic fire-spread simulations. Furthermore, integrated AI frame- works such as Cerberus and CAL FIRE AI combine UAV surveillance, IoT sensor networks, and machine learning algorithms to optimize resource allocation and reduce response times 1 3 Vision-based fire management system using autonomous unmanned… Page 5 of 49 16 (Lehmer and Anguelov 2025; Agrawal 2025). The emergence of domain-specific large lan- guage models, such as WildfireGPT, further supports decision-makers by transforming cli- mate projections and scientific literature into actionable wildfire risk assessments (Xie et al. 2024). Collectively, these innovations represent a paradigm shift in wildfire preparedness and response, offering scalable, intelligent solutions to mitigate the growing threat posed by climate-driven wildfires. UAV-based fire detection has been rising as a new research hot spot due to its various capabilities, including the clear capturing of fire images from challenging, diverse land- scapes and environments, and object tracking (Xu et al. 2025; Haider et al. 2024; Jung et al. 2024). Vision-based fire management systems using UAVs can enable different functions, such as real-time fire detection, estimating the spreading rate, the direction of fire flow utilizing real-world data, and providing cost-effective solutions for firefighting in high-risk areas (Zhang and Jiang 2008; Ma et al. 2024). Early UAV solutions relied on traditional ML models, including support vector machines (SVM), random forests (RF), k-nearest neighbors (k-NN), and decision trees, and were trained on engineered descriptors that encode color ratios, motion or optical-flow patterns, texture such as LBP, shape and perimeter features, or simple ther- mal gradients. These pipelines were attractive for their modest computational cost and are still valuable for edge-constrained platforms and as ensemble components, yet their depen- dence on manual feature design and their limited robustness to illumination changes, haze, occlusions, and cluttered backgrounds constrained generalization in real wildfire scenes. DL addresses these limitations by learning features jointly with the task objective, thereby reducing the need for hand-crafted descriptors and improving robustness across environ- ments. The fundamental structures of modern DL models include convolutional layers with local receptive fields and parameter sharing, non-linear activations, normalization layers for training stability, and down and up-sampling operations to form multi-scale feature pyra- mids. Attention mechanisms can be embedded to modulate channel and spatial responses, and temporal modules, LSTM/GRU, ConvLSTM, or video transformers capture inter-frame dynamics characteristic of smoke onset and flame propagation. Supervised learning domi- nates, with cross-entropy or focal losses for classification and detection and Dice or IoU losses for segmentation; transfer learning and semi/self-supervised strategies are frequently employed to mitigate limited annotation in fire datasets. Within this landscape, convolutional neural networks remain the primary feature extrac- tors for all three perception tasks surveyed here. As backbones such as ResNet, Efficient- Net, MobileNet, CNNs feed task-specific heads for classification of fire and non-fire, while 1 3 Vision-based fire management system using autonomous unmanned… Page 9 of 49 16 encoder-decoder designs such as U-Net and DeepLab produce pixel-accurate segmenta- tion masks that delineate smoke and flame regions for situational awareness and impact assessment. For real-time detection, one-stage YOLO variants are widely adopted on UAV platforms because they deliver single-pass localization with favorable accuracy, latency trade-offs and improved sensitivity to small, distant objects. Attention modules including SE, CBAM, self-attention further suppress distractors such as clouds, glare, and terrain highlights while amplifying discriminative cues like flame cores and thin smoke. Build- ing on attention, transformer architectures for example ViT/Swin backbones, DETR-style decoders, introduce global context that benefits thin-smoke delineation and long-range consistency. In practice, hybrid CNN-transformer designs are often preferred to balance accuracy, memory footprint, and throughput on embedded hardware. Temporal reasoning strengthens operational reliability and supports short-horizon fire-spread prediction. RNN- based modules and video transformers, attached to CNN or transformer features, stabilize detections across frames and reduce false alarms from transient artifacts or camera motion. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) complement these discriminative models by syn- thesizing rare conditions for data augmentation and by enabling cross-modal fusion or trans- lation e.g., RGB to thermal, thereby improving performance under low-light or heavily occluded scenes. For deployment on-board, quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation, and mixed-precision inference are commonly used to meet size, weight, and power con- straints without sacrificing real-time operation. Putting these elements together, a typical UAV perception pipeline ingests multi-modal video (RGB, thermal, multispectral), applies minimal pre-processing and optional registration, and passes the stream to a backbone such as CNN or transformer. Task heads then generate georeferenced bounding boxes (detec- tion), pixel masks (segmentation), and labels (classification); temporal modules refine these outputs before alerting and response. Their ability to deploy quickly, access remote or hazardous zones, and transport diverse sensor payloads makes them indispensable in both pre-fire risk assessment and active fire response (Wang et al. 2025b). UAVs are increasingly used not only to detect fires but also to track their progression and to provide live situational awareness to firefighting teams. Typically, UAVs deployed for fire management follow a systematic operational workflow, beginning with rapid launch and autonomous navagation along predetermined or adaptive paths. During these missions, UAV-based fire management systems typically integrate mul- tiple sensors. High-resolution RGB cameras are used to visually detect flames or smoke, and thermal infrared cameras identify heat signatures even in low-visibility conditions, such as smoke or nighttime (Muksimova et al. 2024). In more advanced configurations, LiDAR sen- sors are also deployed for terrain mapping or structural analysis, supporting navigation and post-fire damage assessment. These multimodal sensors support the detection of diverse fire types, including forest fires, building fires, vehicle fires, and industrial incidents, allowing accurate identification across varied operational contexts. Real-time data analysis, either through onboard edge computing or immediate transmission to ground-based processing stations, enables prompt detection and precise geolocation of fire threats. These capabilities provide actionable insights directly to firefighting teams and incident commanders, enhanc- ing coordination and response effectiveness (Shamta and Demir 2024). The data collected during UAV missions are increasingly processed in real-time using onboard edge computing units. Deep learning models, such as CNNs, YOLO-based object detectors, and vision transformers, are employed to automatically recognize fire patterns, localize fire regions, and classify fire intensity. In advanced systems, generative adversarial networks are also used to enhance or fuse visual and thermal data (Ciprián-Sánchez et al. 2023). This AI-driven processing allows UAVs to function as intelligent aerial platforms, delivering accurate, low-latency analyses and enabling prompt decision-making during emergencies. These systems are designed not only to capture high-resolution visual and thermal data but also to process and transmit actionable fire intelligence in real time, enabling rapid and informed responses across diverse environments. A typical setup involves an autono- mous UAV equipped with a stabilized gimbal camera system, typically integrating dual RGB and thermal sensors and onboard computing hardware for edge AI processing. These UAVs can be preprogrammed to navigate designated surveillance zones via GPS-defined waypoints or dynamically adjust their flight paths using AI-guided mission planning, while continuously transmitting live video streams to ground control stations or conduct- ing onboard inference. Recent advancements have enabled the integration of compact yet high-performance processors, such as NVIDIA Jetson modules, which support real-time deep learning inference directly on the UAV. For instance, a quadcopter system was demon- strated with a Jetson Nano running a YOLOv5 or YOLOv8 model to detect forest fire flames and smoke in real time, sending fire location coordinates and images to a command center (Shamta and Demir 2024). These models enable fast detection and classification of fires with high temporal and spatial precision by processing entire images or video frames in a single feedforward pass. This capability is especially critical in wildfire emergencies, where rapid and accurate detection can significantly influence response time and containment strategies. YOLO models follow a one-stage object detection architecture that directly predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities from input UAV imagery. The input image is first processed by a backbone net- work, such as CSPDarknet, which extracts multilevel feature maps capturing essential fire- related patterns. These features are then refined through a neck module, typically a feature pyramid network (FPN) or path aggregation network (PANet), which enhances multi-scale representation to detect both small fire hotspots and large smoke plumes. The detection head then divides the image into a grid and predicts bounding boxes and class confidence scores for each grid cell in a single pass. Non-max suppression removes overlapping boxes, and the model outputs fire regions with associated certainty levels. These challenges span technical, operational, and ethical domains and significantly affect the reli- ability and scalability of UAV deployments in real-world fire situations. The following sub- sections outline the most critical issues organized by severity and propose corresponding solutions, drawing from recent research and practical deployments. 9.2.1 Dataset imbalance and early-stage fire detection One of the foremost challenges is the lack and imbalance of publicly available fire datasets. Most existing datasets are skewed toward large, fully developed fires, offering insufficient representation of small or early-stage incidents. This imbalance impairs the ability of deep learning models to generalize, particularly in detecting subtle or nascent fire signatures in real-time scenarios (Sun et al. 2025). Consequently, these systems struggle in practice when visibility is limited or when fires are partially obscured. Proposed solutions Data augmentation using generative techniques (e.g., GANs), syn- thetic dataset generation, and the use of transfer learning from large-scale pretrained models can alleviate these constraints. Additionally, incorporating balanced, scenario-rich datasets that capture varied fire intensities and backgrounds is vital for robust model performance. 9.2.2 Environmental variability and multi-modal sensor fusion Environmental conditions, such as wind, fuel type, terrain complexity, and lighting, dra- matically influence the visual and thermal characteristics of fire. These fluctuations often degrade detection accuracy, particularly in heterogeneous or smoke-obscured environments (Zhu et al. 2025a). Enhancing detection accuracy under such variability requires the fusion of RGB, thermal, and in some cases LiDAR data to capture complementary cues. Proposed solutions Multi-modal sensor fusion can help improve system robustness, but it introduces technical complexity in terms of sensor calibration, temporal synchronization, and real-time data integration. Edge-computing architectures and optimized fusion pipe- lines are required to manage computational loads while maintaining responsiveness. 9.2.3 Real-time processing constraints UAVs are inherently constrained by payload capacity, energy limitations, and processing power. Deploying computationally intensive deep learning models onboard is challenging, especially when high-resolution video feeds or multi-sensor data are involved. Lightweight models may reduce latency, but this often comes at the cost of detection accuracy (Abdusa- lomov et al. 2024). Proposed solutions Optimized deep learning models, such as YOLOv5-tiny, MobileNet, along with model compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization), are currently being 1 3 16 Page 36 of 49 S. Danish et al. adopted to mitigate these limitations. Alternatively, edge-cloud hybrid systems can balance the inference load while preserving near real-time responsiveness. 9.2.4 Balancing false positives and false negatives A critical operational challenge is managing the trade-off between false alarms and missed detections. False negatives delay emergency responses, whereas false positives can lead to resource misallocation and unnecessary disruptions (Diaconu 2023). Proposed Solutions: Fine-tuning detection thresholds, implementing ensemble models, and incorporating contextual reasoning (e.g., wind direction, prior fire maps) can help miti- gate both types of errors. Rigorous validation under diverse conditions remains essential. 9.2.5 Privacy and ethical concerns The deployment of UAVs in fire detection and monitoring introduces significant privacy and ethical considerations. UAVs, particularly when equipped with high-resolution cam- eras, may inadvertently capture images of individuals, private property, or sensitive loca- tions during surveillance flights. This is especially problematic in the wildland when urban interface or post-fire damage assessments are conducted, where civilian infrastructure may be visible (Pal et al. 2024). Additionally, centralized training architectures further amplify these challenges by requiring the transmission of raw data to remote servers, increasing the risk of unauthorized access to data and raising further ethical and privacy concerns (Ceviz et al. 2025). Proposed solutions To address these concerns, geofencing techniques can be employed to limit UAV operation over residential zones, and onboard anonymization tools, such as real-time blurring of faces or license plates can help protect privacy. Furthermore, the integration of data governance frameworks and adherence to regional privacy laws (e.g., GDPR, local aviation authority guidelines) is essential. Transparent communication with affected communities and obtaining necessary permissions also foster ethical deployment. Furthermore, the integration of federated learning offers a privacy-preserving alternative to centralized training. In this decentralized framework, UAVs process data onboard and share only model updates, not raw images or sensor data. This approach minimizes data leakage risks, supports compliance with privacy regulations, and leverages onboard computational capabilities for efficient and ethical AI deployment in fire monitoring operations. Addressing these challenges requires a multi-faceted approach involving more compre- hensive and balanced datasets, development of lightweight yet accurate models, real-time sensor fusion frameworks, improved interpretability, and robust error mitigation strategies. Early and accurate detection of fire outbreaks is essential for effective mitigation and timely emergency response. However, conventional fire detec- tion systems face several challenges, including limited spatial coverage, delayed detection, sensitivity to environmental interference, and high false alarm rates. To address these chal- lenges, a variety of approaches have been developed for fire detection, classification, and segmentation. These include sensor-based systems, image processing methods, and more recently, deep learning-based approaches. Among these, the integration of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with vision-based deep learning models has emerged as a promising solu- tion, due to ease of deployment, cost-effectiveness, coverage capability, and ability to oper- ate in dangerous or inaccessible areas. This survey presented a comprehensive review of UAV-based fire management systems, with a focus on vision-driven detection, classification, and segmentation techniques. In par- ticular, we examined the application of advanced deep learning techniques, ranging from convolutional and recurrent neural networks, YOLO variants, to transformers and GANs models and highlighted their effectiveness in enhancing system precision and respon- siveness for fire recognition tasks. Furthermore, we discussed the various types of UAVs employed for fire detection and compiled detailed information on publicly available fire 1 3 16 Page 40 of 49 S. Danish et al. datasets to support and advance further research and development in this field. Despite promising advancements, the field still faces significant challenges. These include limited dataset diversity, real-time processing constraints, environmental variability, and data pri- vacy concerns. Addressing these challenges requires future research to focus on dataset diversity, developing lightweight models for real-time processing, and leveraging multi- modal sensor fusion, federated learning, and vision-language models to enhance detection accuracy. Moreover, interdisciplinary collaboration will be key to driving innovation in this domain. This survey aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers and practitio- ners seeking to advance intelligent UAV-based fire management systems in both research and real-world applications. JSON: Name: vlm_uav_earlyfire Title: A multimodal vision-language transformer with GAN-augmented training for early-stage fire detection from UAV RGB-thermal imagery Short Hypothesis: A multimodal vision-language transformer trained on GAN-augmented aligned RGB-thermal UAV imagery and textual context will achieve a statistically significant increase in recall for early-stage (small/incipient) fires at equal or lower false positive rate compared to a yolov8-based baseline when evaluated on held-out UAV test data. Related Work: Prior work for UAV-based fire perception has focused on three main directions: (1) lightweight one-stage detectors (YOLO variants) for real-time bounding-box detection, (2) CNN/encoder-decoder and transformer-based segmentation models (U-Net variants, TransUNet, Swin) for pixel-wise delineation, and (3) temporal models (RNN/ConvLSTM) and attention modules to stabilize predictions across video. Generative models (GANs / CycleGAN) have been used for data augmentation and RGB↔thermal translation. Existing datasets (FLAME family, FASDD UAV, UAVs-FFDB, M4SFWD, BurnedAreaUAV) provide RGB and some thermal samples but are skewed toward large/visible fires and lack sufficiently annotated early-stage ignition instances. Limitations in current work include: inadequate representation of incipient fires and small smoke plumes, limited use of cross-modal semantic context (textual/mission cues), narrow evaluation on single-modality inputs, insufficient exploration of GAN-augmented training for early-stage detection, and sparse demonstrations of end-to-end vision-language models deployed on UAV-edge hardware under realistic latency constraints. Abstract: Early-stage fire detection from UAV platforms is hindered by scarce training examples of small ignition events, variable environmental conditions, and limited onboard compute. We propose a multimodal approach that integrates a vision-language transformer backbone with aligned RGB and thermal inputs and mission-context text prompts. Training employs GAN-based augmentation to synthesize diverse incipient-fire examples and contrastive alignment to fuse visual and textual cues. The main contribution is a single model that (1) improves sensitivity to early-stage fires by leveraging multimodal context, (2) reduces false positives by conditioning visual predictions on short textual cues (e.g., wind, mission area), and (3) is profiled for edge deployment on representative UAV hardware. Expected outcomes are higher recall for incipient fires and comparable precision to state-of-the-art detectors, with measured inference latency and model footprint compatible with modern UAV edge modules. The approach targets operationally meaningful gains in early warning and situational awareness for UAV-based fire management. Experiments: Datasets: combine FLAME, FLAME2/3, FASDD-UAV, UAVs-FFDB, M4SFWD, BurnedAreaUAV; construct an ‘early-stage’ subset by selecting annotated small/incipient fire instances and augment it with 10k GAN-generated RGB-thermal paired images simulating small flames and thin smoke. Split: 70% train, 15% validation, 15% test ensuring geographic separation. Baselines: (A) yolov8s detector trained on RGB only, (B) yolov8s multi-channel (RGB+thermal) fusion, (C) TransUNet segmentation on RGB+thermal, (D) CNN+LSTM temporal detector (RGB). Proposed Model: multimodal vision-language transformer (MVLT) ingesting RGB patches, thermal patches, and short textual metadata embeddings; trained with cross-entropy detection loss, Dice loss for segmentation head, and contrastive loss for vision-text alignment. Evaluation metrics: recall for early-stage fires, precision, F1-score, mAP@0.5, IoU (segmentation), false positive rate (FPR), time-to-detection (frames and seconds), inference latency (ms) on NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and Jetson Xavier NX, peak memory (MB), and model size (MB). Experiments: (1) Primary comparison: MVLT vs baselines on test set reporting metrics above. (2) Ablations: (i) MVLT without textual input, (ii) MVLT without GAN augmentation, (iii) MVLT using RGB-only, (iv) MVLT with reduced model width (50% params). (3) Temporal stability: evaluate per-frame vs temporally smoothed outputs (5-frame window) and report false positives reduction and detection latency. (4) Cross-domain generalization: train on one geographic region subset and test on a held-out region to report drop in recall and precision. (5) Sensitivity analysis: evaluate performance across varying altitude ranges and lighting (day/night) subsets. Statistical testing: paired bootstrap or McNemar's test to assess significance in recall improvement at α=0.05. Risk Factors and Limitations: Dataset bias: public UAV datasets are skewed toward large fires; synthetic GAN samples may not capture all physics of small ignitions, producing a synthetic-to-real gap. Annotation noise: early-stage labels are ambiguous, causing label noise and reduced maximum achievable recall. Modal alignment: imperfect spatiotemporal alignment between RGB and thermal sensors on real UAV flights can degrade multimodal fusion. Compute and energy constraints: transformer-based multimodal models may exceed practical UAV-edge memory/compute or increase energy draw beyond flight endurance budgets. Real-time latency: meeting strict inference-time constraints on embedded hardware may force model compression that reduces accuracy. Environmental confounders: clouds, fog, dust, and sun-glint can produce high false positives; thin smoke and heat-masked signatures in dense canopy may cause false negatives. Legal/operational constraints: flight permissions, privacy restrictions, and safety protocols may limit data collection and in-situ evaluation. Generalization limits: models trained on specific vegetation types, climate zones, or camera systems may not generalize across ecosystems and sensor configurations.
